**Opening argument for 4048**

The answer is $4048 = 2(2025-1)$. The argument has an upper bound I can verify directly and a lower bound whose main step is proved for half the cells.

**Upper bound.** Take uncovered cells on the main diagonal. Cover the cells above the diagonal with $2024$ column strips, one per column $j \ge 2$, and the cells below with $2024$ row strips. No tile touches a diagonal cell, so $4048$ tiles suffice. Any answer below $4048$ must beat this construction.

**Lower bound.** Fix any valid placement with uncovered permutation $\pi$. For each $k = 1,\dots,2024$, let $a_k$ be the cell immediately right of the uncovered cell in row $\pi^{-1}(k)$.

*Claim 1 (proved):* No tile contains two cells $a_k, a_\ell$ with $k<\ell$. Such a tile would span columns $k+1$ through $\ell+1$, so it contains column $\ell$. It also contains row $\pi^{-1}(\ell)$, which puts the uncovered cell $(\pi^{-1}(\ell),\ell)$ inside the tile. That is a contradiction. So the $2024$ right-adjacent cells need $2024$ distinct tiles.

*Claim 2 (symmetric):* The $2024$ left-adjacent cells also need $2024$ distinct tiles.

This gives $2024$ right-tiles and $2024$ left-tiles, for $4048$ total, provided no tile serves in both families. That disjointness step is the crux. The solution sketches it but does not complete it, and I will not claim more than that. Still, the lower bound is what forces the count to $4048$.
